target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove the work-time barrier for voters, especially low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not generally require private employers to close or to provide paid time off, so many low-income retail and service workers would still have to work and would not reliably get time to vote.

target: AG1's assumption that making Election Day a holiday would necessarily reduce the scheduling barrier enough to help the people most affected.
objection: If workers cannot get guaranteed time off, the key work-time barrier to voting can remain largely intact, especially for low-income workers who are less likely to receive leave from private employers.

target: AG1's premise that a holiday is an effective turnout strategy compared with other reforms.
objection: Research shows election holidays by themselves are not an effective way to increase turnout relative to other voting-access reforms like guaranteed time off or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's comparative-effectiveness objection that the holiday is a worse policy than direct access reforms.
objection: A policy should not be rejected simply because it does not eliminate every barrier or because another reform might be more effective; reducing a major real-world barrier is still a valid reason to support it.

target: AG2's claim that private-employer inaction means the holiday would leave scheduling barriers intact.
objection: A national holiday would still reduce scheduling pressure for schools and many workplaces and could shift broader norms around not working that day, so it can help even if some private employers stay open.

target: AG2's suggestion that school-related constraints are not addressed by a holiday.
objection: Because schools would typically close on a holiday, caregivers and parents would have more practical time to vote, so a holiday would also relieve school-based and childcare-related voting barriers.

target: AG2's suggestion that lack of guaranteed paid leave means the holiday does little for working people.
objection: Polling opportunities already exist outside many standard shifts, and voters can also use early voting or absentee voting where available, so paid leave is not the only way a holiday can help people fit voting into their day.

target: AG1's assumption that many voters have practical time outside work hours to vote.
objection: For many employed adults, Election Day polling hours largely overlap standard weekday work hours, so without flexibility they do not have practical time outside their work shift to vote.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status would meaningfully reduce scheduling barriers for typical workers.
objection: Even if Election Day is a federal holiday, private employers are not required to close or give paid time off, so the scheduling barrier can remain for typical and especially low-income working voters.

target: AG2's argument that OECD precedent is irrelevant because private employers are not uniformly required to give paid leave.
objection: Election-day-on-a-weekend or holiday is already used in many OECD countries, which shows the approach is feasible in real employment settings and should not be dismissed as inherently ineffective.

target: AG2's premise that the holiday fails because it is only a federal holiday.
objection: A federal holiday would still reduce work/school conflicts for many people by causing schools and many workplaces to close or run on reduced schedules, so it would remove a real scheduling barrier.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would help low-income workers by easing caregiving and school-based constraints.
objection: Some school buildings are used as polling places, and if schools are closed or unavailable on a holiday, that can reduce polling locations and make voting harder for some low-income voters.

target: AG1's assumption that closing schools and workplaces is always beneficial for access.
objection: Reduced polling-site availability can force voters to travel farther or wait longer, and low-income voters are more likely to be harmed by those added burdens because they have less transportation and schedule flexibility.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status is not a problem because it cannot remove voting options.
objection: A holiday can remove voting opportunities if it makes commonly used school-based polling places unavailable, so the assumption that it only adds access and never removes it is not guaranteed.

target: AG2's claim that holiday scheduling changes are less direct than school/worktime reductions.
objection: Reducing school and workplace schedule conflicts directly increases practical voting opportunities, particularly for low-income workers who are less flexible and less able to bargain for time off.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not feasible or common enough to count as a serious reform.
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that such scheduling accommodations are a normal and feasible voting-access approach.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status would reduce staffing and create usable time for low-income retail/service workers.
objection: Even on a federal holiday, private employers are not required to close or provide paid leave, so many low-income retail and service workers may still have required shifts that overlap with voting hours.

target: AG1's suggestion that holiday status itself changes work schedules enough to fix the problem.
objection: State laws can directly require employers to grant time off to vote, which is more reliable than hoping a holiday changes employer behavior through the calendar alone.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday meaningfully changes retail/service staffing.
objection: Retail and service staffing is driven by customer demand and operating hours, so a holiday label does not necessarily reduce required work time during polling hours.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status would leave low-income shift workers with more non-work time.
objection: If workplaces remain open and shifts stay largely the same, then a holiday does not reliably create additional non-work time within the voting window for low-income shift workers.

target: AG1's claim that low-income workers would reliably gain practical voting time from a holiday.
objection: Low-income hourly workers often still cannot afford to miss shifts or take unpaid time away, so even if some overlap is reduced they may not have usable time to vote.

target: AG1's claim that overlap reduction alone makes voting time reliable for low-income workers.
objection: If workers still face wage loss or schedule risk because paid or job-protected leave is not guaranteed, then a holiday does not reliably ensure practical access to voting for them.

target: AG2's claim that lack of job-protected leave means a holiday cannot help workers finish voting.
objection: A holiday often gives many workers a much larger block of time off, not just a brief gap, so they may have enough time to travel, wait, and complete voting despite the lack of guaranteed leave.

target: AG1's claim that most low-income workers would have their free window expanded enough to cover most of Election Day.
objection: Because many low-income workers remain scheduled during daytime hours and private employers are not required to reduce shifts, their overlap with polling hours may remain essentially unchanged.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would leave workers enough usable free time to vote.
objection: If required work time still overlaps much of the period when polls are open, low-income workers would not generally gain a free window that covers most of the day.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is reliable enough to justify itself as a voting-access reform.
objection: A reform that is not reliable for low-income workers and that leaves them exposed to wage loss or inflexible schedules is worse than enforceable access reforms like state-mandated time off to vote.

target: AG1's claim that reduced overlap usually gives enough time for workers to complete voting.
objection: Voting can take more time than just arriving at the polls, because travel, ID/check-in, and waiting can be lengthy, so reducing overlap alone does not ensure workers can complete the process.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status reliably translates into completed voting for low-income workers.
objection: Even if a holiday reduces some work time, workers may still have too little free time to finish voting without risking job consequences or leaving before they are done.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is a reliable practical access reform for low-income workers.
objection: Because a holiday is less reliable than enforceable state time-off-to-vote rules, it disadvantages low-income workers relative to more direct and enforceable access reforms.
